newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF mulls allowing govt affiliates to issue bonds.
newsitem.headline: MOF mulls allowing govt affiliates to issue bonds.

text.p: Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) is considering allowing government-affiliated financial institutions and other government-affiliated bodies to issue bonds, a MOF official said on Monday.
However, the official added that nothing concrete had so far been decided.

"With the development of financial markets, the funding system of government-affiliated institutions is being reviewed. Allowing them to issue bonds on their own would be one of the options. The idea is to introduce market mechanisms where possible," the MOF official said.

The leading Japanese economic daily, Nihon Keizai Shimbun, reported in its Sunday edition that MOF was considering allowing the National Forestry Management Programme to issue bonds of around 30-year maturity next fiscal year from April 1.
The MOF official said the Finance Ministry was still only studying the idea following a request from the agriculture minister.

Most of the institutions concerned are currently financed by the government Fiscal Investment and Loan Programme (FILP), which collects money from the postal savings system and public pension funds through MOF's Trust Fund Bureau.
The bureau, in turn, lends money to the institutions through the FILP.
Currently, some government-affiliated agencies issue government-guaranteed bonds, but these are issued under the same terms, regardless of differences in financial conditions.

Politicians and analysts say the institutions, many of which are running at a deficit, should be more cost-conscious and efficient and that introducing market mechanisms into their fund raising would be one way to improve their efficiency.
